title: Windows Exception-Driven Control Flow and Anti-Debugging
html:
Windows Exception-Driven Control Flow and Anti-Debugging

A protected Windows program can use an intentional exception as a branch: the faulting instruction is only the entry to a handler that selects the next user-code address. This hides edges from linear disassembly and moves the next step into exception dispatch.[1]

Dispatch matters

A debugger attached to the process receives a first-chance exception before application handlers. If it passes the event as unhandled, Windows searches the process's handlers; an exception with no handler returns to the debugger as last-chance. A debugger that consumes a breakpoint or single-step event can therefore change whether the program's handler runs.[2]

AddVectoredExceptionHandler(1, handler) registers a process-wide VEH at the front of the vectored list. It runs before frame-based SEH, but a later first-priority registration can move another handler ahead of it. Returning EXCEPTION_CONTINUE_SEARCH leaves the exception for other handlers; EXCEPTION_CONTINUE_EXECUTION resumes from the saved CONTEXT, including any register changes made by the handler.[3][4][7]

Classic x86 SEH uses stack-linked registrations, which !exchain can inspect. Native x64 uses RUNTIME_FUNCTION entries in .pdata with unwind data in .xdata, not that x86 chain. Do not apply the x86 SEH overwrite workflow to a native x64 process.[5][6]

Turn a fault into a control-flow edge

For example, a zero divisor can deliberately raise EXCEPTION_INT_DIVIDE_BY_ZERO rather than represent a bug. The handler must recognize the exception and fault address, then set ContextRecord->Rip (or Eip on x86) to a valid continuation before returning EXCEPTION_CONTINUE_EXECUTION.[5][7][10]

xor ecx, ecx
div ecx                 ; deliberate fault, not a normal fall-through

The handler core below assumes fault_site and continuation are known addresses in the same control-flow context. A real implementation must preserve the expected stack and registers, and must not resume at the same faulting instruction or it will fault again.[7]

if (e->ExceptionRecord->ExceptionCode == EXCEPTION_INT_DIVIDE_BY_ZERO &&
    e->ExceptionRecord->ExceptionAddress == fault_site) {
#ifdef _M_X64
    e->ContextRecord->Rip = (DWORD64)continuation;
#else
    e->ContextRecord->Eip = (DWORD)continuation;
#endif
    return EXCEPTION_CONTINUE_EXECUTION;
}
return EXCEPTION_CONTINUE_SEARCH;

The same mechanism can consume an intentional INT3/__debugbreak() (EXCEPTION_BREAKPOINT) and redirect execution. Do not blindly increment Rip to "skip the breakpoint": the saved address and required adjustment depend on the trap, instruction encoding, and debugger behavior. Compare ExceptionRecord->ExceptionAddress with the saved instruction pointer and disassemble the bytes before choosing the continuation.[8] The Vectored Overloading loader is a separate hardware-breakpoint example that changes a loader syscall's return state.

Trap Flag as a debugger-dependent gate

Bit 0x100 in EFLAGS/RFLAGS is the Trap Flag (TF). Setting it makes the next instruction boundary raise STATUS_SINGLE_STEP (0x80000004). A VEH or SEH branch can distinguish a single-step event passed to the application from one consumed by a debugger, but this is a heuristic controlled by debugger exception policy, not reliable proof that a debugger exists.[2][8][9]

pushfq
or qword ptr [rsp], 100h
popfq

If the handler only wants one step, clear 0x100 in the resumed context's EFlags before continuing. Also distinguish TF-driven steps from hardware-breakpoint events by checking the triggering address and debug state; both can appear as EXCEPTION_SINGLE_STEP.[8][9] For WinDbg's sxe, sxd, and sxi first-/second-chance settings, see WinDbg exception automation.
